Rehana, you asked what kept me awake, and it was not the numbers. It was that I had signed off the earlier reports myself. I kept asking, if something was wrong in those, am I part of it? Did I miss it, or did I look away? Those are different questions, and I needed to answer them honestly before I pointed at anybody else.

So I pulled out my old sign-offs and checked what I had actually seen at the time. Then I booked an hour with a lawyer to ask how to disclose my own part properly. I'm Vandana, and I'll be honest, that hour was uncomfortable. But when I wrote my report, my own role was in the first paragraph, and nothing could surprise me later.

passage:
I'm Ira, and Pallavi and I joined the audit firm in the same batch. Last month she found a problem in a client's stock valuation, the kind that had been going on for at least two quarters.
What I noticed was that she didn't rush to report it that evening. She sat at her desk with the old files and went very still. I asked what was wrong.
'I signed off the stock sheets in the last review,' she said quietly. 'I checked the counts but not the prices. So am I part of this?'
She spent the next day listing exactly what she had checked and what she hadn't, with dates. Then she booked a session with the firm's legal counsel and asked how to disclose her own earlier sign-off in the same report.
She told me later the counsel said honesty now was far better than someone finding it later. Her report went in with a short paragraph about her own role.
I don't know if she slept that week. But she didn't leave her own name out of her report.

qa.q: What had Pallavi checked in the last review?
qa.a: The counts but not the prices.

qa.q: What does Pallavi going very still suggest?
qa.a: She was shaken and worried, suddenly afraid her own earlier sign-off made her part of the problem.

qa.q: Why was disclosing her own role in the report wise?
qa.a: It avoided a nasty surprise later and showed honesty, which the legal counsel said was far better than being found out.

qa.q: How does Pallavi's reaction look to Ira?
qa.a: Ira sees her pause and reflect instead of rushing, and respects that she didn't hide her own part.

grounding: Shows an auditor asking whether earlier sign-offs make her part of a problem and getting legal advice on disclosing her own role.

Monday. Pankaj finds that a client's travel expenses have been inflated for a year. He opens the audit file to note it, and freezes. Two of those quarters carry his own initials as reviewer. He had ticked them without checking the receipts.
Wednesday. He can't stop thinking about it, so he takes it to Lalit, a senior he trusts, over chai. 'If I report this, do I have to say I missed it?' Lalit asks, 'What happens if you don't, and someone finds your initials later?' Pankaj is quiet for a while. 'Then it looks like I was hiding it. Or part of it.' He books time with the firm's legal team for Friday.
Friday. The legal adviser listens and explains how to set out his own role plainly: what he reviewed, what he didn't, and when. Pankaj writes the report that evening, including a paragraph that begins, 'I reviewed the Q1 and Q2 files and did not verify receipts.' His hands feel cold as he presses send, but his chest feels lighter.

qa.q: Whose initials were on two of the quarters?
How does Pankaj feel on Monday when he sees his initials?
qa.a: He freezes, suddenly anxious and ashamed that a missed check links him to the problem.

qa.q: What made the Friday meeting useful?
qa.a: The legal adviser helped Pankaj set out his role plainly, so the report was honest about what he had and hadn't checked.

qa.q: How might Lalit see Pankaj's question over chai?
qa.a: Lalit sees a worried junior tempted to leave something out, and helps him think it through with a single question.

grounding: Shows an auditor realising his earlier sign-offs connect him to a problem and seeking legal advice on how to disclose his own role.
